chunks.text:
Caching — What a cache is

A cache is a small, fast store that holds copies of results that are expensive to
produce, so that repeat requests can be served without redoing the work. The expensive
work might be a database query, a call to another service, or a computation.

Caching pays off when the same data is requested repeatedly and changes less often than
it is read. If every request asks for different data, a cache adds latency and memory
cost while returning nothing useful.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.text:
Caching — Cache hits and misses

A **cache hit** occurs when the requested data is already in the cache and can be
returned immediately, without touching the underlying source. A **cache miss** occurs
when the data is not present, so the system must fetch it from the original source —
typically the database — and usually store it in the cache on the way back, so the next
request for the same data is a hit.

The **hit rate** is the fraction of requests served as hits. It is the single most
important cache metric, because it determines how much of the expensive work is actually
avoided. Effective latency is roughly:

```
average latency = hit_rate × cache_latency + (1 − hit_rate) × source_latency
```

With a 1ms cache and a 50ms database, a 90% hit rate gives about 5.9ms average. Raising
it to 95% gives about 3.45ms. The relationship is nonlinear: at high hit rates, small
improvements in hit rate matter a great deal, because misses dominate the average.

A miss is slightly *more* expensive than having no cache at all, since the system pays
the cache lookup before the database read. Caches win on the average, not on every
request.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.text:
Caching — Where caches live

Caching happens at several layers, and they compose.

- **Browser cache** — the client stores responses, governed by `Cache-Control` headers.
  The cheapest possible hit: no network at all.
- **CDN / edge cache** — shared geographic caches holding static assets and cacheable
  responses near users.
- **Application cache** — an in-process or shared store such as Redis or Memcached,
  holding query results, session data or computed values.
- **Database cache** — the database's own buffer pool, keeping hot pages in memory.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.text:
Caching — Caching strategies

**Cache-aside (lazy loading)** is the most common. The application checks the cache
first; on a miss it reads the database and writes the result into the cache. Only
requested data is cached, but every first request pays a miss, and cache and database can
drift apart.

**Write-through** writes to the cache and the database together on every write. The cache
stays consistent, but writes are slower and data that is never read still gets cached.

**Write-behind** writes to the cache immediately and to the database asynchronously.
Writes are fast, but a crash before the flush loses data.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.text:
Caching — Invalidation and eviction

Cached data goes stale as the underlying source changes, and a cache has finite memory.
Two mechanisms address these separately.

**Expiry (TTL)** attaches a lifetime to each entry; after it passes, the entry is treated
as a miss. TTL is the blunt but reliable tool: it bounds how stale data can be without
requiring the system to detect changes. A short TTL means fresher data and a lower hit
rate.

**Explicit invalidation** deletes or updates an entry when the source changes. Fresher
than TTL, but it requires every write path to know which cache keys it affects — and
missing one produces data that is wrong indefinitely.

**Eviction** is what happens when the cache fills up. LRU (least recently used) discards
the entry untouched for the longest, and is a good default because it approximates "what
is unlikely to be requested again."

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.text:
Caching — Failure modes

**Thundering herd (cache stampede).** A popular key expires and hundreds of concurrent
requests all miss and all hit the database at once. Mitigated by allowing only one
request to recompute while others wait, or by refreshing slightly before expiry.

**Cache penetration.** Requests for keys that do not exist in the source are never
cacheable, so every one reaches the database. Mitigated by caching the negative result.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.text:
Caching — Exercise: Choose a strategy

A product page shows a price that changes at most twice a day and a stock count that
changes every few seconds. Both are read thousands of times per minute. Propose a caching
approach for each field, state the TTL you would choose, and explain what a user would
observe if you applied your price strategy to the stock count.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1 (caching discussion)

chunks.section: Why queries get slow without an index
chunks.text:
Database Indexing — Why queries get slow without an index

To answer `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@b.com'` without an index, the database
has no way to know where matching rows live. Its only option is a **full table scan**:
read every row in the table and test each one against the condition. On a table of ten
million rows, that means reading ten million rows to return one.

The cost grows linearly with table size. A query that returns in 5ms on a development
database with a thousand rows can take several seconds in production against the same
code and the same query, purely because the table grew. This is the single most common
cause of a query that "suddenly" became slow without anyone changing it.

metadata.source: Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke — Ch. 1 (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

chunks.section: What an index is and why it speeds queries up
chunks.text:
Database Indexing — What an index is and why it speeds queries up

An index is a separate, sorted data structure that maps column values to the locations
of the rows containing them. Most relational databases use a **B-tree**, a balanced tree
kept in sorted order.

Because the tree is sorted, the database can find a value by comparison instead of by
scanning: check the root, follow the one child whose range contains the target, repeat.
Each step discards most of the remaining data. This makes lookup cost **logarithmic**
rather than linear — O(log n) instead of O(n).

The practical difference is large. Finding one row among ten million takes roughly 23
comparisons in a B-tree, versus ten million row reads in a full scan. **This is why
adding an index improves query performance: it converts a linear scan of every row into
a small number of targeted reads.**

A B-tree index also keeps values in sorted order, so the same structure accelerates
range queries (`WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01'`), sorting (`ORDER BY`), and finding
minimum or maximum values — not just exact-match lookups.

metadata.source: Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke — Ch. 1 (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

chunks.text:
Database Indexing — What indexes cost

Indexes are not free, which is why databases do not simply index everything.

- **Write cost.** Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update every affected index as
  well as the table. A table with six indexes does roughly seven times the write work.
- **Storage.** An index duplicates the indexed columns plus row pointers. Indexes on a
  heavily indexed table can exceed the size of the table itself.
- **Planner cost.** More indexes means more options for the query planner to evaluate,
  and more opportunities for it to choose badly.

The trade-off is therefore read speed against write speed and storage. Indexing is a
decision about a workload, not a universal improvement. A write-heavy audit log and a
read-heavy product catalogue deserve opposite answers.

metadata.source: Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke — Ch. 1 (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

chunks.section: When an index will not help
chunks.text:
Database Indexing — When an index will not help

An index on a column is only usable if the query lets the database compare against the
indexed values directly.

- **Functions on the column.** `WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com'` cannot use a plain index
  on `email`, because the index stores the original values, not the lowercased ones.
- **Leading wildcards.** `WHERE name LIKE '%smith'` cannot use a B-tree, because sorted
  order tells you nothing about suffixes.
- **Low selectivity.** An index on a boolean `is_active` column where 95% of rows are
  true saves little: the database still reads most of the table, and may reasonably
  decide a scan is cheaper than the index lookup plus row fetches.
- **Wrong column order in a composite index.** An index on `(country, city)` supports
  filtering by `country`, or by `country` and `city` together, but not by `city` alone.
  The leftmost columns must be used for the rest to be reachable.

metadata.source: Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke — Ch. 1 (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

chunks.text:
Database Indexing — Reading a query plan

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE <query>` shows what the database actually did. The distinction to look
for is the access method: `Seq Scan` means a full table scan, `Index Scan` means the
index was used to find specific rows, and `Index Only Scan` means the query was answered
from the index alone without touching the table at all.

A `Seq Scan` on a large table in a query that filters to a few rows is the signature of a
missing or unusable index.

metadata.source: Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke — Ch. 1 (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

chunks.text:
Database Indexing — Exercise: Diagnose the slow query

An `orders` table has 12 million rows and an index on `(customer_id, created_at)`. This
query takes 4 seconds:

```sql
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at > '2024-01-01' ORDER BY created_at;
```

Explain why the existing index does not help. State what you would add. Then explain
what the write-path cost of your change would be, and name one situation in which you
would decide not to add it.

metadata.source: Markus Winand, Use The Index, Luke — Ch. 1 (https://use-the-index-luke.com/)

chunks.section: What replication is and why it is used
chunks.text:
Database Replication — What replication is and why it is used

Replication keeps copies of the same data on more than one database machine. It serves
three distinct purposes, and confusing them leads to bad designs:

- **Read capacity** — reads can be spread across copies.
- **Availability** — if one machine dies, another holds the data.
- **Locality** — a copy near users in another region reduces latency.

Replication does not help with write capacity. Every write must eventually reach every
replica, so the write load on each machine is unchanged. Scaling writes is what
partitioning (sharding) is for, and the two are solutions to different problems.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.text:
Database Replication — Leader and follower

The most common arrangement is **leader–follower** (also called primary–replica). One
node is the leader and accepts all writes. Every write is recorded in a replication log
and sent to the followers, which apply the changes in the same order. Followers accept
reads but never writes.

This arrangement is popular because it is simple and avoids write conflicts entirely:
with exactly one writer, there is never a question of which of two concurrent writes to
the same row wins.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.section: Read replicas: when to use one
chunks.text:
Database Replication — Read replicas: when to use one

A **read replica** is a follower used to serve read traffic. It is the right tool when
the workload is read-heavy and the reads can tolerate slightly stale data.

Good candidates: analytics and reporting queries, dashboards, search result pages,
recommendation feeds, exports and any expensive aggregate that would otherwise compete
with production traffic on the leader.

Poor candidates: reading a value immediately after writing it, anything where a user
must see the effect of their own action, and financial or inventory checks where a stale
read causes a real error. These reads should go to the leader.

A read replica is also not the fix for a slow query. If a query is slow because it scans
a large table, it will be equally slow on the replica; the replica only stops it from
slowing down everything else. Fix the query or the index first, then decide whether to
move the traffic.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.text:
Database Replication — Synchronous and asynchronous replication

In **synchronous** replication, the leader waits for a follower to confirm the write
before reporting success. No data is lost if the leader fails, but write latency now
includes the follower, and if the follower stalls, writes stall with it.

In **asynchronous** replication, the leader reports success immediately and ships changes
to followers afterwards. Writes are fast and follower problems do not block them, but
writes confirmed to the client can be lost if the leader fails before they propagate.

**Semi-synchronous** is the common compromise: wait for one follower, let the rest catch
up asynchronously.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.section: Replication lag and what it looks like
chunks.text:
Database Replication — Replication lag and what it looks like

Asynchronous replicas are behind the leader by some amount of time — the **replication
lag**. Usually milliseconds; under heavy write load or a long-running query on the
replica, it can reach seconds or minutes.

Lag produces specific, confusing bugs:

- **Read-your-own-writes.** A user updates their profile, the next page reads a replica
  that has not caught up, and their change appears to have vanished. Fix: route reads
  that follow a user's own write to the leader for a short window.
- **Monotonic reads.** Two successive reads hit replicas with different lag, and the
  user sees time move backwards. Fix: pin a user's reads to one replica.

Replication lag is a metric to alert on, not an implementation detail. A replica lagging
by minutes is serving data that may be wrong enough to matter.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.text:
Database Replication — Failover

If the leader fails, a follower must be promoted. This requires detecting the failure,
choosing a replacement, and redirecting writes. With asynchronous replication, the new
leader may be missing the most recent writes, which are then lost. Automatic failover can
also produce **split brain**, where two nodes both believe they are the leader and accept
conflicting writes.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.text:
Database Replication — Exercise: Route the reads

An e-commerce backend has one leader and two asynchronous read replicas lagging about
200ms. Decide where each of these reads should go, and justify each in one sentence:
(a) the homepage product listing, (b) a user's cart immediately after they add an item,
(c) the monthly revenue report, (d) the stock check during checkout.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 5, Replication

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — What an HTTP request is

HTTP is a request/response protocol. A client sends a request to a server, the server
returns a response, and the connection concern ends there. Every request carries four
things: a method, a path, a set of headers, and an optional body.

A minimal request looks like this:

```
GET /users/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
```

The method says what the client wants to do. The path identifies the resource. Headers
carry metadata such as content type, authentication and caching directives. The body
carries data, and is empty for methods like GET.

HTTP is stateless. The server does not remember anything about a previous request from
the same client. Any continuity — a login session, a shopping cart — has to be carried
explicitly in each request, usually in a cookie or an Authorization header.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP)

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — HTTP methods

GET retrieves a resource and must not change server state. POST submits data and
typically creates something. PUT replaces a resource entirely. PATCH modifies part of a
resource. DELETE removes it.

Two properties matter when reasoning about methods. A method is **safe** if it does not
modify state: GET is safe, POST is not. A method is **idempotent** if making the same
request many times has the same effect as making it once: GET, PUT and DELETE are
idempotent, POST is not. Idempotency is why a client can safely retry a failed PUT but
not a failed POST — retrying a POST may create a duplicate record.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP)

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Status codes

Status codes are grouped by their first digit.

- **2xx — success.** 200 OK is a successful request. 201 Created means a new resource
  was made. 204 No Content means success with nothing to return.
- **3xx — redirection.** 301 is a permanent move, 302 a temporary one. 304 Not Modified
  tells the client its cached copy is still valid.
- **4xx — client error.** 400 Bad Request means the request was malformed. 401
  Unauthorized means the client is not authenticated. 403 Forbidden means it is
  authenticated but not allowed. **404 Not Found means the requested resource does not
  exist on the server.** 429 Too Many Requests means the client is rate limited.
- **5xx — server error.** 500 Internal Server Error is an unhandled failure on the
  server. 502 Bad Gateway and 503 Service Unavailable usually indicate a problem
  upstream or an overloaded service.

The 4xx/5xx split matters operationally: 4xx means the client must change something,
5xx means the server is at fault and the client may reasonably retry.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP)

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Headers and content negotiation

Headers let client and server agree on the shape of the exchange without changing the
URL. `Accept` tells the server what formats the client can handle; `Content-Type` tells
the receiver what format the body actually is. `Authorization` carries credentials.
`Cache-Control` governs how long a response may be reused.

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP)

chunks.text:
HTTP Fundamentals — Exercise: Read a failing request

A client repeatedly sends `POST /orders` and receives `500 Internal Server Error`. The
client retries automatically five times. Answer three questions: Is it safe for the
client to retry this request? What would change if the endpoint returned 400 instead?
What single property of POST makes the retry risky here?

metadata.source: MDN Web Docs — HTTP overview (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP)

chunks.text:
Load Balancing — Why load balancing exists

A single server has a ceiling: CPU, memory, connections. Once traffic approaches it,
latency climbs and the server eventually fails. There are two responses. **Vertical
scaling** makes the machine bigger — simple, but bounded by the largest machine money can
buy, and it leaves a single point of failure. **Horizontal scaling** adds more machines,
which is effectively unbounded but requires something to distribute traffic across them.

That something is a load balancer: it accepts incoming requests and forwards each to one
of several backend servers. It delivers two benefits at once — capacity, because work is
spread out, and availability, because a failed server can be removed from rotation while
the rest keep serving.

metadata.source: NGINX — HTTP Load Balancing guide (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html)

chunks.text:
Load Balancing — Distribution algorithms

**Round robin** sends each request to the next server in sequence. Simple and fair when
servers are identical and requests cost about the same.

**Weighted round robin** assigns each server a share proportional to its capacity, for
when the fleet is not uniform.

**Least connections** sends each request to the server with the fewest active
connections. Better than round robin when request durations vary widely, because it
responds to actual load rather than assuming uniformity.

**Hash-based (e.g. by client IP or request path)** sends the same key to the same server
consistently. Useful when a server holds local state or a warm local cache for that key.
The cost is that adding or removing a server reshuffles assignments — which is what
consistent hashing is designed to limit.

metadata.source: NGINX — HTTP Load Balancing guide (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html)

chunks.text:
Load Balancing — Health checks

A load balancer must know which backends are usable, or it will keep routing traffic into
a failed server.

**Passive** checks observe real traffic and remove a backend after repeated errors or
timeouts. No extra load, but detection requires real requests to fail first.

**Active** checks poll a dedicated endpoint (`GET /healthz`) on a fixed interval and
remove backends that stop responding correctly. Failures are detected before users see
them, at the cost of constant background traffic.

A good health endpoint checks that the instance can actually serve — including its
database connection — but must not be so thorough that a slow dependency takes the whole
fleet out of rotation at once.

metadata.source: NGINX — HTTP Load Balancing guide (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html)

chunks.text:
Load Balancing — Layer 4 and Layer 7

**Layer 4** balancing routes on TCP information — IP address and port — without reading
the request. It is fast and protocol-agnostic, but cannot make decisions based on content.

**Layer 7** balancing reads the HTTP request and can route on path, header, cookie or
method: `/api/*` to one pool, `/images/*` to another. It enables TLS termination,
per-route rate limiting and request rewriting, at the cost of more work per request.

metadata.source: NGINX — HTTP Load Balancing guide (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html)

chunks.text:
Load Balancing — Sessions and statelessness

Round-robin distribution breaks if a server keeps session state in local memory, because
the user's next request may land elsewhere and appear logged out.

**Sticky sessions** pin a user to one server. This works but undermines even
distribution, and the session is lost when that server dies. The better answer is to make
backends **stateless**: keep session data in a shared store such as Redis, or in a signed
token held by the client. Then any server can serve any request, and losing a server
costs nothing but capacity.

metadata.source: NGINX — HTTP Load Balancing guide (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html)

chunks.text:
Load Balancing — Exercise: Diagnose uneven load

A fleet of six identical servers sits behind a round-robin load balancer. Two servers run
at 90% CPU while four sit near 20%. All health checks pass. Give two distinct
explanations consistent with these symptoms, say what you would measure to tell them
apart, and propose the change you would make for each.

metadata.source: NGINX — HTTP Load Balancing guide (https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html)

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Resources and URL structure

A REST API models a system as a set of **resources**, each addressable by a URL. The
central design move is that URLs name things, not actions. `/users/42/orders` is a
resource. `/getUserOrders?id=42` is a remote procedure call wearing a URL costume.

Conventional structure uses plural nouns and nests to show ownership:

```
GET    /orders          list orders
POST   /orders          create an order
GET    /orders/42       fetch one order
PATCH  /orders/42       modify part of it
DELETE /orders/42       remove it
GET    /users/7/orders  orders belonging to user 7
```

The verb lives in the HTTP method, never in the path. If you find yourself writing
`/orders/42/cancel`, the question to ask is whether cancellation is really a state
change on the order (`PATCH /orders/42` with `{"status":"cancelled"}`) or genuinely a
new resource (`POST /orders/42/cancellations`). Both are defensible; `/cancel` as a verb
in the path is the option that breaks the model.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Request and response design

Responses should be predictable in shape. A collection endpoint returns a list plus
pagination metadata; a single-resource endpoint returns the object. Keeping the envelope
consistent means clients can write one parsing path instead of one per endpoint.

Errors deserve as much design attention as success cases. An error response should carry
a machine-readable code, a human-readable message, and enough context to act on:

```json
{ "error": { "code": "insufficient_stock",
             "message": "Only 2 units of SKU-119 remain",
             "field": "items[0].quantity" } }
```

Returning `200 OK` with `{"success": false}` is a common mistake. It forces every client
to inspect the body to learn whether the call worked, and it defeats every piece of
infrastructure — proxies, monitoring, retry logic — that reasons about status codes.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Versioning

Any API with external consumers will need to change incompatibly at some point.
Versioning in the path (`/v1/orders`) is the most common approach because it is visible,
easy to route, and easy to reason about in logs. Header-based versioning keeps URLs
stable but makes debugging harder because the version is invisible in a browser.

The important discipline is distinguishing breaking from non-breaking changes. Adding an
optional field is non-breaking. Removing a field, renaming one, or tightening validation
is breaking and needs a new version.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Pagination

Returning an unbounded list is a latency and memory problem waiting to happen.
**Offset pagination** (`?limit=20&offset=40`) is simple but degrades on large offsets,
because the database must still walk past every skipped row, and it can skip or repeat
items when rows are inserted between requests.

**Cursor pagination** (`?limit=20&after=eyJpZCI6NDJ9`) passes an opaque pointer to the
last item seen. It stays fast at any depth and is stable under concurrent inserts, at the
cost of not being able to jump to an arbitrary page.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5

chunks.text:
REST API Design — Exercise: Critique an endpoint

An API exposes `POST /api/getUsersByStatus` which accepts `{"status": "active"}` and
returns `200 OK` with `{"success": true, "data": [...]}` — all 40,000 matching users.
List four separate design problems with this endpoint and give the corrected version of
each. State which single change you would make first and why.

metadata.source: Roy Fielding, Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures, Ch. 5

chunks.text:
System Design and Trade-offs — There is no best architecture

System design questions rarely have a correct answer independent of context. They have
answers that are correct *given* a set of requirements, constraints and expected load.
The same design that is right for ten thousand users is wrong for ten million, and the
design that is right for ten million is wasteful and slow to build for ten thousand.

The skill being exercised is not recalling architectures. It is deciding which properties
matter for this system, and being explicit about what is being given up in exchange.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable Applications

chunks.text:
System Design and Trade-offs — The properties worth trading

Most backend decisions move along a small number of axes, and improving one usually costs
another.

- **Latency** — how long one request takes. Distinguish the average from the tail: p99
  latency determines what the unluckiest users experience, and averages hide it.
- **Throughput** — how much work the system handles per unit time. A system can have
  excellent throughput and terrible tail latency at the same time.
- **Cost** — machines, storage, bandwidth, and the engineering time to build and operate.
- **Reliability** — continuing to work correctly when parts fail. Usually bought with
  redundancy, which costs money and adds coordination.
- **Consistency** — whether everyone sees the same data at the same time. Often traded
  for latency and availability, as replication makes concrete.
- **Complexity** — the cost paid forever afterwards, in debugging, onboarding and
  operations. Frequently ignored in design discussions and frequently the one that hurts.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable Applications

chunks.section: How to reason about a design decision
chunks.text:
System Design and Trade-offs — How to reason about a design decision

A defensible decision follows a recognisable shape.

1. **State the requirement in numbers.** "Fast" is not a requirement; "p99 under 200ms at
   5,000 requests per second" is. Without numbers there is no way to tell whether a
   design succeeds.
2. **Find the actual bottleneck.** Measure before changing. The slow part is often not
   the part that looks slow.
3. **Name at least two options.** A decision with one option is not a decision.
4. **State what each option costs.** Every option has a cost; if you cannot name it, you
   have not understood the option.
5. **Choose, and record why.** The reasoning is more valuable later than the choice, both
   for the next engineer and for knowing when the decision should be revisited.
6. **Say what would change your mind.** Which metric crossing which threshold means this
   decision should be reopened.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable Applications

chunks.text:
System Design and Trade-offs — Common trade-offs in practice

**Caching** trades freshness for latency and load. You accept data that may be slightly
stale in exchange for speed, and pay in invalidation complexity.

**Replication** trades consistency for read capacity and availability. Asynchronous
replicas serve more reads and survive failures, but can return stale data.

**Indexing** trades write speed and storage for read speed, which is why databases do
not index every column by default.

**Horizontal scaling** trades simplicity for capacity and resilience. More machines mean
more capacity and no single point of failure, but also distribution, coordination and a
harder debugging story.

**Asynchronous processing** trades immediacy for responsiveness. Moving work into a
background job returns to the user faster, but the result is no longer available at the
moment of the request, and failures must be handled somewhere the user cannot see.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable Applications

chunks.text:
System Design and Trade-offs — Estimating before building

Rough numbers eliminate whole designs early. If 10,000 daily active users each make 20
requests, that is 200,000 requests a day — about 2.3 per second on average, and perhaps
20 at peak. That fits comfortably on one modest server, and any design proposing a
distributed architecture for it is solving a problem that does not exist.

Order-of-magnitude estimates are usually enough. The purpose is not precision; it is
knowing whether the answer is 2 requests per second or 20,000.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable Applications

chunks.text:
System Design and Trade-offs — Exercise: Defend a decision

A service serving 500 requests per second has a p99 latency of 800ms. Profiling shows 600
of those milliseconds in a database aggregate query on a table that grows daily. You have
two weeks and no budget for new infrastructure.

Propose two different approaches, state the cost of each along the axes above, choose
one, and name the metric that would tell you your choice was wrong.

metadata.source: Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications — Ch. 1, Reliable, Scalable, Maintainable Applications
